title: Roots and the Qal qatal

objectives.can: Recognise a Qal qatal form and give its person, gender and number.
Recognise ten of the commonest verbs.

explanation.summary: Hebrew verbs are built on roots of three consonants. The root carries the core meaning, and vowels and endings carry the grammar. The qatal is the conjugation that adds person, gender and number as endings to a stem. It presents an action or a state as a whole, and it is often, but not always, translated as a past tense.

sections.heading: Roots, stems and the dictionary form
body: Most Hebrew words, not only verbs, are formed from a root of three consonants. The root שׁ מ ר has to do with keeping and guarding. Around it, different vowels and affixes make different words: שָׁמַר 'he kept', שֹׁמֵר 'keeping' or 'a keeper', יִשְׁמֹר 'he will keep' or 'he keeps', שְׁמֹר 'keep!', לִשְׁמֹר 'to keep'. A lexicon lists a verb under its Qal 3rd masculine singular qatal, which is the simplest form, and the corpus does the same. That form is the headword.
Qal is the basic verbal stem. Other stems change the meaning in different ways, and they are the subject of later lessons.

sections.heading: Qatal is the suffix conjugation
body: The conjugation takes its name from the root ק ט ל, 'kill', used by grammarians as a model; in this course we use real verbs. The qatal is called the suffix conjugation because person, gender and number are marked by endings: שָׁמַרְתִּי 'I kept', שָׁמַרְתָּ 'you (masculine singular) kept'. The next conjugation, the yiqtol, marks person with a prefix, and you will meet it in the next lesson.

The traditional English name for qatal is the 'perfect'. The 3rd masculine singular has no ending at all. The other forms add an ending to the stem, and the stem often changes its vowel as it does so: compare שָׁמַר with שָׁמְרָה 'she kept' and שָׁמְרוּ 'they kept'. The first vowel reduces to a shewa when an ending that begins with a vowel is added.

sections.heading: What the qatal says
body: Qatal is not 'the past tense'. A common way to describe it is that it presents an action or state as a whole, seen from the outside, without looking at how it unfolds. Because of this it is often used for what is finished, and so it is often translated by the English past: God 'created' the heavens, a man 'heard' a voice. But the same form is also rendered 'I have given', 'I know', or even 'I will give', as the context requires.

Compare three verses. In Genesis 3:10 שָׁמַעְתִּי reports something heard earlier: 'I heard'. In Genesis 22:12 יָדַעְתִּי is a present state resulting from what has just happened: 'now I know'. In Genesis 15:18 נָתַתִּי is a promise stated as already settled: translators write 'I have given' or 'I give' or 'I will give'. Read the form for the whole action and let the clause and the story tell you the time.

sections.heading: Stative verbs
body: Some verbs describe a state or a quality, such as being old, fearing or being able. In the Qal their 3rd masculine singular qatal has a different vowel, usually ē or ō in the second syllable: זָקֵן 'he was old' or 'he became old', יָרֵא 'he feared'. With a state verb, qatal is often best translated by an English present: זָקַנְתִּי is 'I am old' or 'I have grown old'.
The ordinary action verbs, such as שָׁמַר, have a patah (a) in that syllable. The vowels of the stem differ between the two classes, but the endings are the same.

sections.heading: Reading a form
body: Look at the end of the word first. -תִּי is 'I', -תָּ is 'you' (masculine), -נוּ is 'we', -תֶּם is 'you' (plural), -ָה is 'she', and -וּ is 'they'. The 3rd person plural has one form for both genders, and the 1st person has one form for both genders. Then see the stem and find the root: the three consonants that are not part of the ending.

misunderstandings: Qatal is not the past tense. It is the form used for completed action and for states, and it is often translated as a past tense, but it is also used for the present perfect, for present states, and for promises. Let the context decide.
A root has no vowels. The root of שָׁמַר is the three consonants שׁ מ ר. Vowels belong to the forms made from it.
The ending -ָה on a qatal is not the noun ending of the same shape. It marks the 3rd feminine singular. The verb is told by its stem and by its place in the clause.
The 3rd plural -וּ is the same for masculine and feminine. Do not look for a feminine plural form in the 3rd person.

deeper.heading: Tense or aspect?
body: S. R. Driver, whose treatise on the tenses is listed among the sources of this course, described the Hebrew perfect as presenting an action as complete. Other scholars argue that the qatal is basically a past tense, or that it marks one point of view in discourse. The question is disputed, and this course treats the qatal as a form whose use is learned from the texts rather than as an English tense in disguise.
